explanations.answer: In the assembly of the godly
explanations.explanation: That's the spot, baker. The psalm says, "Sing to the LORD a new song—His praise in the assembly of the godly." So this song isn't a solo in the shower. It's a gathering of people praising Him together. Bring your voice, even if it cracks.
Gates are a fair guess, baker. But this psalm never mentions them. It says the new song is for "…the assembly of the godly." (Psalm 149:1). The praise happens where God's people gather.

Wilderness is a real place in the Bible, baker, and David wrote a psalm from there (Psalm 63, title). But Psalm 149 doesn't send the song out into the desert. It says "…His praise in the assembly of the godly." (Psalm 149:1). So the song is for God's people gathered together.
True, baker! Psalm 149:3 says, "Let them praise His name with dancing…" Dancing is right there in the text. The psalm puts it first, before the tambourine and harp. I'd give it a hop myself.

Plot twist, baker: it's true. Psalm 149:3 says, "Let them praise His name with dancing, and make music to Him with tambourine and harp." So dancing is part of the praise. The psalm doesn't say to sit still and look serious.

explanations.answer: The LORD takes pleasure in His people
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. Psalm 149:4 says, "For the LORD takes pleasure in His people…" Read that one slowly. He's not just putting up with them. He takes pleasure in them, and that's why the dancing and the music make sense.

explanations.answer: The harvest has finally come in
explanations.explanation: A good harvest would be a fine reason for a party, baker. But the psalm never mentions one. The reason it gives is in verse 4: "For the LORD takes pleasure in His people…" The praise comes from who He is to them, not from a full barn.

I see why you'd think that, baker, since the psalm talks about nations and peoples later on. But the reason for the praise comes first, and it's simpler. Psalm 149:4 says, "For the LORD takes pleasure in His people…" The singing starts there.

I get why riches sounds right, baker. But the psalm doesn't say that. Psalm 149:4 says, "He adorns the afflicted with salvation." So what the LORD puts on them is salvation, and that beats any pile of gold.
False is right, baker. Psalm 149:4 says, "He adorns the afflicted with salvation." No riches in that verse. It's salvation, and I'd trade a drawer full of gold for that any day.
Yes, the saints, baker. Psalm 149:5 says, "Let the saints exult in glory; let them shout for joy upon their beds." So the shouting for joy is for them. Joy gets a loud voice here, and I like it.

Close, baker, but the nations show up later in the psalm, and in a very different spot (Psalm 149:7). The ones told to exult and shout for joy are the saints. Psalm 149:5 says, "Let the saints exult in glory…"

The elders are a fair guess, baker, but this psalm never names them. Verse 5 says, "Let the saints exult in glory; let them shout for joy upon their beds." So the saints are the ones doing the shouting. Elders can join in, but that's not what the text says.

That's the one, baker. Psalm 149:6 says, "May the high praises of God be in their mouths, and a double-edged sword in their hands…" Praise in the mouth and a sword in the hand, side by side. It's a heavy picture, and the next verses say what the sword is for.

A scroll sounds like a peaceful pick, baker, but the psalm doesn't mention one. Psalm 149:6 says, "May the high praises of God be in their mouths, and a double-edged sword in their hands…" The sword is what the verse puts in their hands.

A cup would be a gentler picture, baker, and I'd hold it happily. But the psalm says something else. Psalm 149:6 says, "…a double-edged sword in their hands…" That's why the verses after it get so heavy.

True, baker, and it's a heavy line. The psalm says the sword is "…to inflict vengeance on the nations and punishment on the peoples…" (Psalm 149:7). It's right there in the text. I think this one is worth sitting with for a moment.

It's true, baker. Psalm 149:6-7 says, "a double-edged sword in their hands, to inflict vengeance on the nations and punishment on the peoples." The text says it plainly. This is one of the heavy parts.
Yes, kings, baker. Psalm 149:8 says, "…to bind their kings with chains and their nobles with shackles of iron…" Kings in chains and nobles in iron shackles. It's a hard picture, so take it slowly.

Priests are a reasonable guess, baker, but they aren't in this verse. Psalm 149:8 says, "…to bind their kings with chains and their nobles with shackles of iron…" The ones bound with chains are kings.

Prophets feel like they'd fit in a list like this, baker, but the psalm doesn't name them here. Psalm 149:8 says, "…to bind their kings with chains and their nobles with shackles of iron…" The word you want is kings.
That's the one, baker. Psalm 149:9 says, "…to execute the judgment written against them." The psalm calls it a judgment that is written. It's a heavy line, so I'll leave it right there.

explanations.answer: A judgment of their own choosing
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. The psalm doesn't call it a judgment of their own choosing. Psalm 149:9 says, "…to execute the judgment written against them." The judgment it names is the one that is written.

explanations.answer: A judgment voted on by the elders
explanations.explanation: No vote in this psalm, baker. No committee either. Psalm 149:9 says, "…to execute the judgment written against them." The judgment is already written, and the elders aren't mentioned.
